Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 97, verses 1–5:

(p-657) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Qadr

The scholars differed concerning the place of revelation of this surah. Ibn 'Abbas and others said it is Madani; Qatadah said it is Makki.

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿Indeed, We revealed it during the Night of Decree.﴾ ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.﴾ ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord, with every matter.﴾ ﴿Peace it is until the rising of the dawn.﴾

The pronoun in "anzalnahu" (We revealed it) refers to the Qur'an, although it has not been mentioned previously, because the meaning points to it. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said: Allah the Exalted revealed it on the Night of Decree to the lowest heaven all at once, then sent it down piecemeal upon Muhammad ﷺ over twenty years. Al-Sha'bi and others said: the meaning is: We began sending down this Qur'an to you on the Night of Decree. It has been narrated that the descent of the angel at Hira' was in the last ten nights of Ramadan, so this interpretation is consistent. It has also been narrated that the descent of the angel was on the fourteenth of Ramadan, and then this interpretation is not consistent except according to the view of those who say that the Night of Decree rotates through the whole month and is not confined to the last ten nights of Ramadan. Others said: the meaning of the Exalted's words, ﴿Indeed, We revealed it during the Night of Decree﴾, is: We revealed this surah concerning the matter of the Night of Decree and its virtue. Since the surah is part of the Qur'an, the pronoun came referring to the Qur'an as an expression of glorification and embellishment.

The Exalted's words "fi laylat" (during a night) are like the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: "I feared that a Qur'an would be revealed concerning me on the night of the revelation of Surat al-Fath," and like the saying of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, in the hadith of the slander: "I consider myself too insignificant that a Qur'an should be revealed concerning me." The Night of Decree is a night that Allah the Exalted singled out with great virtue, and made better than a thousand months in which there is no Night of Decree; this was said by Mujahid and others. (p-658) This virtue was granted to this Ummah when Muhammad ﷺ saw the lifespans of his Ummah and found them short.

The Exalted's words ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ are an expression of glorification of it. Then He Exalted explained it afterward with His words: ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.﴾ Ibn 'Uyaynah said in the Sahih of al-Bukhari: whatever in the Qur'an is (wa ma adraka), Allah has informed him of it; and whatever in it is (wa ma yudrika), he was not informed of it.

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others mentioned that it was named the Night of Decree (laylat al-qadr) because Allah the Exalted decrees therein the terms of life, the provisions, and all the events of the world, and hands that over to the angels to carry out. Something similar has been narrated concerning the night of the middle of Sha'ban, and there are apparent indications of this in the Book of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, such as the Exalted's words: ﴿Therein every wise matter is made distinct﴾ [al-Dukhan: 4]. As for a definitively established authenticity, it is not present. Al-Zuhri said its meaning is: the Night of great station, honour and magnitude of affair, from your saying: "a man who has qadr" (a man of standing). Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it was named the Night of Decree because it bestows upon whoever keeps vigil in it a great standing he did not have before, and makes him great in the sight of Allah the Exalted. It was also said: it was named so because all the work done in it has a weighty qadr.

The Night of Decree is sought in the odd nights of the last ten nights of Ramadan; this is the sound view on which reliance is placed. It falls on odd nights according to whether the month is complete or deficient. Therefore, the one who awaits it should watch for it from the twentieth night onward every night until the end of the month, because the odd nights in a complete month are not the odd nights in a deficient one. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "On the third remaining, on the fifth remaining, on the seventh remaining," and he, upon him be prayer and peace, said: "Seek it in the third, the fifth, the seventh and the ninth." Malik said: he means by the ninth the night of the twenty-first. Ibn Habib said: Malik meant that if the month is deficient. The apparent meaning of this is that he, peace be upon him, was cautious regarding both complete and deficient months, and this is not achieved except by keeping vigil over all ten nights. It was narrated from Abu Hanifah and a group that the Night of Decree has been lifted, but this view is rejected; rather, only its specific identification has been lifted. Ibn Mas'ud said: whoever establishes the entire Sunnah will attain it. Abu Razin said: it is the first night of the month of Ramadan. Al-Hasan said: it is the night of the seventeenth, the night on whose morning the Battle of Badr occurred. Many scholars said: it is the night of the twenty-third, the night of 'Abdullah ibn Unays al-Juhani, and Ibn 'Abbas said this. Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the Companions also said: it is the night of the twenty-seventh. Ibn 'Abbas supported his view by the fact that man was created from seven and his sustenance is placed in seven, and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them all, approved of this. Zayd ibn Thabit and Bilal said: it is the night of the twenty-fourth. Some scholars said: Allah the Exalted hid it from His servants so that they would strive in worship and not rely upon its virtue and neglect other nights.

Then Allah the Exalted magnified the matter of the Night of Decree, like His words: ﴿And what can make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 3], and other than that. Then He Exalted informed that it is better for one who performs a deed in it than a thousand months, which is eighty years (p-660) and three years and a third of a year. It was narrated from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when he was reproached for handing over the affair to Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, he said: "Allah the Exalted showed His Prophet ﷺ in a dream the sons of Umayyah leaping upon his pulpit like monkeys leaping, and he was troubled by that, so Allah the Exalted gave him the Night of Decree, which is better than the duration of the Umayyad rule, and informed him that they would rule for this period of time."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Then the unseen was disclosed that from the Sunnah of the community until the killing of Marwan al-Ja'di was exactly this period of time, although the statement is contradicted by the fact that the Umayyads ruled in the west of the earth for a period other than this. In the Sahih, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Decree in faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven."

"Al-Ruh" (the Spirit) is Jibril, peace be upon him. It was also said: they are a category of the guarding angels, peace be upon them. As for the Exalted's words ﴿by permission of their Lord, with every matter﴾, people differed. Whoever says "in this night the affairs are decreed for the angels" says: this descent is for that, and "min" (from/with) is for the beginning of the end, i.e., their descent is for the sake of these decreed matters and because of them. "Salam" is then the predicate of a new beginning, i.e., peace is this night until the beginning of its day; this is the view of Nafi' al-Maqburi, al-Farra' and Abu al-'Aliyah. Some said: "min" has the meaning of "ba'" (with), i.e., with every matter. Whoever does not say "the affairs are decreed in that night" says: the meaning of the verse is: the angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord with mercy, forgiveness and bounties. Then he made the Exalted's words "from every matter" connected to His words, glorified is He: "Peace it is," i.e., from every frightening matter from which one ought to be safe, it is peace. Mujahid said: no disease afflicts anyone therein. Al-Sha'bi and Mansur said: "salam" means greeting, i.e., the angels greet the believers (p-661) with salutation. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and al-Kalbi read: "min kulli imri'" (from every man), i.e., one is safe therein from every evil person; this is based on "salam" meaning "salamah" (safety). It was narrated from him that "salaman" means "tahiyyah" (greeting), and "kullu imri'" is meant as the angels, i.e., from every angel a greeting upon the believers; this is for those who worship therein. Those who hold that the speech ends at the Exalted's words "salam" say that the Exalted's words "hiya" are only an indication that it is the night of the twenty-seventh of the month, since this word is the twenty-seventh of the words of the surah. Ibn Bakir, Abu Bakr al-Warraq and al-Naqqash mentioned this purpose from Ibn 'Abbas.

The majority of the seven readers read "hatta matla'a" with a fatha on the lam; al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash, Abu Raja', Ibn Muhaysin and Talhah read "hatta matli'a" with a kasra on the lam. It was said: both are verbal nouns with one meaning in the dialect of Banu Tamim. It was also said: with fatha it is a verbal noun, and with kasra it is the place of rising according to the people of the Hijaz. The reading with fatha has merits on this view; the other reading is explained as a figurative usage, as if the time is confined to that place and completed in it. The kasra is also justified on another ground: that some verbal nouns of this form have come with kasra, such as "al-mu'jizah," and their saying "'alahu al-mukabbir" (with fatha on the mim and kasra on the ba'), and from it "al-mahid" (menstruation), so "al-matla'" is treated as a verbal noun in the manner of what is anomalous. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "Salam hiya ila matla'i al-fajr."

The tafsir of Surat [al-Qadr] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 97, verses 1–5:

(p-657) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Qadr

The scholars differed concerning the place of revelation of this surah. Ibn 'Abbas and others said it is Madani; Qatadah said it is Makki.

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿Indeed, We revealed it during the Night of Decree.﴾ ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.﴾ ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord, with every matter.﴾ ﴿Peace it is until the rising of the dawn.﴾

The pronoun in "anzalnahu" (We revealed it) refers to the Qur'an, although it has not been mentioned previously, because the meaning points to it. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said: Allah the Exalted revealed it on the Night of Decree to the lowest heaven all at once, then sent it down piecemeal upon Muhammad ﷺ over twenty years. Al-Sha'bi and others said: the meaning is: We began sending down this Qur'an to you on the Night of Decree. It has been narrated that the descent of the angel at Hira' was in the last ten nights of Ramadan, so this interpretation is consistent. It has also been narrated that the descent of the angel was on the fourteenth of Ramadan, and then this interpretation is not consistent except according to the view of those who say that the Night of Decree rotates through the whole month and is not confined to the last ten nights of Ramadan. Others said: the meaning of the Exalted's words, ﴿Indeed, We revealed it during the Night of Decree﴾, is: We revealed this surah concerning the matter of the Night of Decree and its virtue. Since the surah is part of the Qur'an, the pronoun came referring to the Qur'an as an expression of glorification and embellishment.

The Exalted's words "fi laylat" (during a night) are like the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: "I feared that a Qur'an would be revealed concerning me on the night of the revelation of Surat al-Fath," and like the saying of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, in the hadith of the slander: "I consider myself too insignificant that a Qur'an should be revealed concerning me." The Night of Decree is a night that Allah the Exalted singled out with great virtue, and made better than a thousand months in which there is no Night of Decree; this was said by Mujahid and others. (p-658) This virtue was granted to this Ummah when Muhammad ﷺ saw the lifespans of his Ummah and found them short.

The Exalted's words ﴿And what can make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ are an expression of glorification of it. Then He Exalted explained it afterward with His words: ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.﴾ Ibn 'Uyaynah said in the Sahih of al-Bukhari: whatever in the Qur'an is (wa ma adraka), Allah has informed him of it; and whatever in it is (wa ma yudrika), he was not informed of it.

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others mentioned that it was named the Night of Decree (laylat al-qadr) because Allah the Exalted decrees therein the terms of life, the provisions, and all the events of the world, and hands that over to the angels to carry out. Something similar has been narrated concerning the night of the middle of Sha'ban, and there are apparent indications of this in the Book of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, such as the Exalted's words: ﴿Therein every wise matter is made distinct﴾ [al-Dukhan: 4]. As for a definitively established authenticity, it is not present. Al-Zuhri said its meaning is: the Night of great station, honour and magnitude of affair, from your saying: "a man who has qadr" (a man of standing). Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it was named the Night of Decree because it bestows upon whoever keeps vigil in it a great standing he did not have before, and makes him great in the sight of Allah the Exalted. It was also said: it was named so because all the work done in it has a weighty qadr.

The Night of Decree is sought in the odd nights of the last ten nights of Ramadan; this is the sound view on which reliance is placed. It falls on odd nights according to whether the month is complete or deficient. Therefore, the one who awaits it should watch for it from the twentieth night onward every night until the end of the month, because the odd nights in a complete month are not the odd nights in a deficient one. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "On the third remaining, on the fifth remaining, on the seventh remaining," and he, upon him be prayer and peace, said: "Seek it in the third, the fifth, the seventh and the ninth." Malik said: he means by the ninth the night of the twenty-first. Ibn Habib said: Malik meant that if the month is deficient. The apparent meaning of this is that he, peace be upon him, was cautious regarding both complete and deficient months, and this is not achieved except by keeping vigil over all ten nights. It was narrated from Abu Hanifah and a group that the Night of Decree has been lifted, but this view is rejected; rather, only its specific identification has been lifted. Ibn Mas'ud said: whoever establishes the entire Sunnah will attain it. Abu Razin said: it is the first night of the month of Ramadan. Al-Hasan said: it is the night of the seventeenth, the night on whose morning the Battle of Badr occurred. Many scholars said: it is the night of the twenty-third, the night of 'Abdullah ibn Unays al-Juhani, and Ibn 'Abbas said this. Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the Companions also said: it is the night of the twenty-seventh. Ibn 'Abbas supported his view by the fact that man was created from seven and his sustenance is placed in seven, and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them all, approved of this. Zayd ibn Thabit and Bilal said: it is the night of the twenty-fourth. Some scholars said: Allah the Exalted hid it from His servants so that they would strive in worship and not rely upon its virtue and neglect other nights.

Then the unseen was disclosed that from the Sunnah of the community until the killing of Marwan al-Ja'di was exactly this period of time, although the statement is contradicted by the fact that the Umayyads ruled in the west of the earth for a period other than this. Some said: "min" has the meaning of "ba'" (with), i.e., with every matter. Whoever does not say "the affairs are decreed in that night" says: the meaning of the verse is: the angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord with mercy, forgiveness and bounties. Then he made the Exalted's words "from every matter" connected to His words, glorified is He: "Peace it is," i.e., from every frightening matter from which one ought to be safe, it is peace. Ibn Bakir, Abu Bakr al-Warraq and al-Naqqash mentioned this purpose from Ibn 'Abbas.
